question: What is the main goal of planning a personal diet for a patient?

options.A: Reducing hospital food costs for the facility
options.B: Turning nutritional science into daily food choices
options.C: Eliminating all carbohydrates from the diet
options.D: Ensuring every patient eats the exact same calories

explanation: You're doing great! Diet planning simply takes nutrition rules from the textbook and translates them into the actual meals a person enjoys every day.

question: Why can't nurses just use one standard diet plan for every single patient?

options.A: Because physical, metabolic, and lifestyle needs vary greatly among people
options.B: Because doctors legally cannot approve identical diets for two patients
options.C: Because food guides require a different plan for every day of the year
options.D: Because standard hospital menus never contain enough protein

explanation: Spot on! Every patient has a unique body, age, and lifestyle, so their meal plan needs to match who they are.

question: In nutrition, what does the term DRI stand for?
explanation: DRIs are just the standard reference values health workers use to check if someone is getting enough nutrients.

question: What is the main job of the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)?

options.A: To show the minimum amount of food needed to avoid fatigue
options.B: To determine the cheapest food sources of essential vitamins
options.C: To warn against taking dangerously high amounts of a nutrient
options.D: To calculate the exact number of calories burned during rest

explanation: Think of the UL as a safety warning light. It tells us the highest amount of a nutrient a person can take before it starts causing harm, especially from supplements.

question: Which of these is a classic example of an anthropometric measurement?
explanation: You've got this! Anthropometric just means measuring physical body dimensions like height, weight, and BMI.

question: You notice a patient has dry, brittle hair, pale skin, and spoon-shaped nails. What part of the nutritional assessment is this?
explanation: When you look directly at the patient's body for physical signs of nutrition issues, you are doing a clinical observation!

question: Why do we use visual food guides, like the healthy eating plate?

options.A: To replace the need for professional medical consultations
options.B: To promote expensive imported food items over local produce
options.C: To help clients build balanced meals easily without complex math
options.D: To guarantee that every person loses weight within one week

explanation: Pictures make nutrition easy! Visual guides help patients build healthy meals at a glance without stressing over numbers.

question: According to the healthy plate method, what portion of a meal should be fruits and vegetables?
explanation: Filling half the plate with colorful fruits and veggies is a quick, easy rule to make sure a meal is full of fiber and vitamins.

question: Why is it important to respect a patient's cultural background when planning their meals?

options.A: Because medical science proves cultural foods are superior
options.B: To prevent the client from ever eating carbohydrates
options.C: Because hospital policy strictly forbids serving foreign foods
options.D: To ensure the client is willing and able to follow the meal plan long-term

explanation: People eat what they love! When we respect cultural food preferences, patients are much more likely to stick to their diet.

question: A patient cannot afford expensive imported foods listed on a standard diet sheet. What should you do as their nurse?

options.A: Tell them to stop worrying about nutrition and just eat less food
options.B: Discharge the patient without any dietary plan
options.C: Suggest nutritious, affordable, and culturally familiar local food alternatives
options.D: Insist that they find extra money to buy the prescribed imported items

explanation: Great nursing judgment! Always adapt care to fit the patient's pocket by recommending budget-friendly, local Nigerian food options.

question: What simple hand guide can a patient use to estimate a single portion of meat or protein?
explanation: Your hand is always with you! Using the palm is a handy, quick trick for patients to gauge a normal protein serving.

question: What usually happens when someone skips meals all day and eats one massive meal at night?

options.A: Blood sugar spikes and digestive strain
options.C: Faster weight loss and improved metabolism

explanation: Good to know! Overloading the stomach all at once confuses digestion and causes sudden jumps and crashes in blood sugar.

question: Why do nurses need to review and update diet plans from time to time?

options.A: Because patients get bored eating the same foods for more than three days
options.B: Because hospital regulations require rewriting charts weekly
options.C: Because food items change their vitamin content every single month
options.D: Because client needs, health status, and life circumstances change over time

explanation: Life isn't static, and neither is health! Regular checks ensure the diet plan keeps up with the patient's changing body and life.

question: A client on a weight-loss diet says they are always hungry and haven't lost any weight after four weeks. What should you do?

options.A: Tell the client to stop eating all solid food until the next appointment
options.B: Discharge the client from care for failing to lose weight
options.C: Review the current food intake and adjust the plan collaboratively with the client
options.D: Ignore the feedback because four weeks is not enough time to evaluate

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Sit down with the patient, figure out what's blocking progress together, and tweak the plan so it actually works for them.
